# Moving section logarithms: zero-face and normal classification

This note proves a geometric restriction on the section defect retained
in `candidate 4dd22db8fd75566e`.
It does not discard supporting allocations. In fact a previously known
truncated-triangle sequence has nonzero section defect even when every
prelimit cut is proper.

The main new statements are: a positive section anchor alone gives
uniform logarithmic integrability, with no intrinsic inball; and under
the actual compact finite-plane presentation, nonzero section defect
forces the limiting cap plane to be the zero plane of a limiting affine
component of (L\). Hence it exposes an entire zero face of the fiber.

## 1. Exact hypotheses, including the affine presentation

Work first in one continuous fiber of dimension (d\ge1\). Let positive
convex bodies (K_j\to K\) in Hausdorff distance stay in a common ball,
with (K\) full-dimensional. Let positive concave (L_j\) converge
uniformly on the relevant compact range to a continuous (L\ge0\),
positive in the interior of (K\). Assume

\[
 \sup_j\int_{K_j}\frac{dx}{L_j(x)}<\infty.          \tag{1}
\]

For the stronger normal classification assume a fixed finite bound (R\)
on the number of affine components, and a presentation, after passing
to a subsequence,

\[
 L_j=\min_{1\le r\le R} A_{rj},\qquad
 A_{rj}(x)=b_{rj}+c_{rj}\cdot x\longrightarrow A_r(x)
                     =b_r+c_r\cdot x.            \tag{2}
\]

Components never active on the current fiber may be discarded. No
unproved implication from arbitrary uniform convergence to (2) is used.
In the current selected-source framework, (2) follows from the stated
source/contact bounds: each chosen affine majorant touches a source
with an own-fiber ball of radius (r_s\), and its value there is at most
a uniform (C\). Its continuous gradient therefore has norm at most
(C/r_s\). If it is active somewhere on the current bounded fiber, its
intercept on that fiber is bounded too. The number of chosen source
planes is uniformly finite. Relabeling and subsequences then give (2),
without requiring any bound on irrelevant base slopes.

Let

\[
 \Pi_j=\{u_j\cdot x=t_j\},\quad
 (u_j,t_j)\to(u,t),\quad |u_j|\ge b_*>0,
 \quad D_j=K_j\cap\Pi_j.                         \tag{3}
\]

Let (\lambda_j\) be any actual allocated coarea measure bounded by

\[
 0\le\lambda_j\le |u_j|^{-1}\mathcal H^{d-1}|_{D_j}.
                                                               \tag{4}
\]

This includes full proper sections and all inside/outside allocations.
Assume the ordinary joint section/selector limit is retained and the
negative-log weighted masses are bounded, as proved by the capwise
Gauss–Green argument in the dependency. Its defect is denoted (s_H\).
Every assertion below also applies independently at each of finitely
many sampled bases, replacing (t_j\) by (t_j-a_j\cdot z\).

## 2. A positive anchor gives intrinsic log uniform integrability

Let (D\) be any (m\)-dimensional compact convex set, (m\ge1\), with
nonnegative concave function (F\), and let (x_0\in D\) satisfy
(F(x_0)\ge c>0\). For (0<t<c\), homothety toward (x_0\) gives

\[
 x_0+(1-t/c)(D-x_0)\subset\{F\ge t\}.
\]

Indeed every point on the left is ((t/c)x_0+(1-t/c)x\), where
(F(x)\ge0\). Therefore

\[
 |\{F<t\}|_m
 \le[1-(1-t/c)^m]|D|_m
 \le\frac{m|D|_m}{c}\,t.                         \tag{5}
\]

The anchor may be on the boundary. No inball, slope bound, or lower
bound for (|D|_m\) is needed. For (ell=(-\log F)_+\), (5) gives,
for sufficiently large (B\),

\[
 \int_{\{\ell>B\}}\ell
 \le\frac{m|D|_m}{c}(B+1)e^{-B}.                 \tag{6}
\]

The layer-cake formula here includes the term (B|\{\ell>B\}|\).
Apply this to (D_j,L_j\). Bounded outer diameter bounds the intrinsic
section areas, so any sequence of section anchors with (L_j\ge c\)
gives uniform log integrability for the full geometric sections and,
by (4), for every actual allocation. Hence (s_H=0\).

If (d=1\), the section is a point and the same conclusion follows
directly from its uniformly positive value.

## 3. Proper limit sections have no defect; a defect collapses to zeros

If the limiting plane intersects the interior of (K\), choose an
intersection point where (L>0\). Its small interior ball ensures a
nearby point of (D_j\) with parameter bounded below. Thus **every
limiting proper section has (s_H=0\)**. This conclusion does not need
the finite-plane presentation (2), only the convergence and positivity
assumptions of Section 1.

More generally, after a subsequence of nonempty sections, let
(D_j\to D\) in Hausdorff distance. If any point (x\in D\) has
(L(x)>0\), approximate it by (x_j\in D_j\) and use (6). Thus

\[
 s_H\ne0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D\subset\{L=0\}.
                                                               \tag{7}
\]

Under (2), the zero set has dimension at most (d-2\) (and is empty
when (d=1\)). Here are the details. Fatou on the eventually included
interior points of (K\) gives (int_K1/L<\infty\) from (1). Each
(A_r\) is nonnegative on (K\), and

\[
 \{L=0\}=\bigcup_r[K\cap\{A_r=0\}].
\]

If one of these exposed faces had dimension (d-1\), join a
positive-area relative facet patch to an interior point. In the
resulting cone (A_r\) is proportional to normal distance from that
patch, and (int1/A_r\) diverges as (int_0 ds/s\). Since
(L\le A_r\), this contradicts (int1/L<\infty\). The same argument
at an interval endpoint handles (d=1\).

Consequently (7) implies

\[
 \mathcal H^{d-1}(D_j)\to0,\qquad \lambda_j(D_j)\to0. \tag{8}
\]

For completeness, identify the moving planes with their limit by
convergent rigid maps. A bounded convex set converging to one of
dimension below (d-1\) lies in a slab of vanishing width in that
intrinsic space, which proves the area convergence. No logarithmic
weighted-mass conclusion follows from (8) alone.

## 4. Stronger classification: the cap plane must be a zero support plane

Assume (d\ge2\) and (2). Suppose no limiting component (A_r\)
vanishes identically on the limiting plane (Pi\). Then (s_H=0\).

To prove it, restrict each component to (Pi_j\). There are two cases.

* Its limiting tangential gradient on (Pi\) is nonzero. For large
  (j\), that gradient has norm at least some (gamma_r>0\). Since
  (A_{rj}>0\) on (D_j\), the set (D_j\cap\{A_{rj}<t\}\) lies in
  an intrinsic slab of width at most (t/\gamma_r\). Fubini and the
  common outer ball give intrinsic area at most (C_rt\).
* Its limiting tangential gradient is zero. Its value on (Pi\) is
  then a constant. This constant is nonnegative if the (D_j\) are
  nonempty, by taking any convergent sequence of their points. It is
  strictly positive by the assumption of this paragraph. Hence
  (A_{rj}\) has a uniform positive floor on all (D_j\).

There are only finitely many components. Since
({L_j<t\}\cap D_j=\bigcup_r\{A_{rj}<t\}\cap D_j\), these estimates
give a uniform (Ct\) sublevel-area bound for small (t\). The same
layer-cake argument as (6) proves log uniform integrability.

Its contrapositive is the promised normal classification:

\[
 s_H\ne0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \Pi=\{A_r=0\}\text{ for at least one limiting component }r.
                                                               \tag{9}
\]

The component cannot be identically zero on the whole fiber, because
(L>0\) in its interior. Thus (c_r\ne0\), and

\[
 u\parallel c_r,\qquad
 F=K\cap\Pi\subset\{L=0\},\qquad \dim F\le d-2. \tag{10}
\]

In particular the **whole exposed fiber face** in the limiting cap
plane is zero, not merely the subset reached by a collapsing sequence
of sections. The possible unoriented continuous normals form a subset
of the finite list (\{\mathbb Rc_r:c_r\ne0\}\). This conclusion is
fiberwise; it does not assert that the ambient base-tilt plane is a
global zero plane of (L\) on every sampled fiber.

Either orientation in (10) can occur. With one orientation the limiting
cap contains all of (K\), and with the other it contains only the zero
face. No supporting allocation has been set to zero in this argument.

## 5. Nonzero defect survives collapsing PROPER sections

Use the actual truncated-triangle calibration already recorded in
`candidate 4dd22db8fd75566e`,
§6. Write

\[
 a=1/m,\quad \eta=2^{-m},\quad
 K_m=\{x,y\ge0:a\le x+y\le1\},\quad
 \widetilde L_m=x+y-a+\eta.
\]

The limit is the standard triangle with (L=x+y\). The exact inverse
integral is

\[
 \int_{K_m}\frac{dx\,dy}{\widetilde L_m}
 =1-a+(a-\eta)\log\frac{1-a+\eta}{\eta}
 \le1+\log2.                                    \tag{11}
\]

Here (0<\eta\le a\) and (1-a+\eta\le1\). Thus all inverse integrals
are uniformly bounded. The affine gradients are fixed and the
convergence is uniform.

Now choose the **proper** cap plane

\[
 x+y=a+\eta^2,
\]

with raw continuous normal (u=(1,1)\). It is proper for every large
(m\); no allocation choice is involved. Its full coarea mass is
(a+\eta^2\), whereas the parameter is constant there, equal to
(\eta+\eta^2\). Hence

\[
 \int_{D_m}(-\log\widetilde L_m)\,
       \frac{d\mathcal H^1}{\sqrt2}
 =(a+\eta^2)[m\log2-\log(1+\eta)]\longrightarrow\log2. \tag{12}
\]

The unweighted coarea tends to zero and the entire section collapses
to the zero vertex. The limiting plane (x+y=0\) is exactly the zero
plane of (L\), as (9) requires. Reversing the cap orientation leaves
the section defect unchanged. Thus proper prelimit cuts may converge
to either inside or outside supporting incidence with nonzero defect.

Multiplying (\widetilde L_m\) by its geometric normalizer does not
change this defect: the normalizers converge to (e^{1/2}\), and the
extra bounded logarithm is multiplied by vanishing section mass. The
same calibration has uniformly interior actual one-row contact means,
as recorded in the dependency. It is not claimed to be a globally
critical or deepest-source cap family.

## 6. What this supplies to the capwise flux

In Defect's exact identity

\[
 -\pi_*(n a_H)=M\sum_i c_i\zeta_i^H-u_Hs_H,
\]

the section correction vanishes on every limiting proper fiber section.
Every possible nonzero correction is confined to a collapsed zero-face
incidence, and its continuous normal is parallel to a limiting
finite-plane gradient by (9). This is stronger geometric information
than merely (operatorname{supp}s_H\subset\{L=0\}\).

It does not prove that these corrections cancel after averaging the
cap law, that their allocations equal closed-cap bits, or that the
boundary/inverse-volume defects vanish. Example (12) prohibits
discarding them merely because their unweighted sections disappear.
